blocks.text: First, the authority of the Greeks and of Jerome, who consistently explain it so. I do not think it safe to depart from them unless there are weighty reasons, and here [II, 455] I see none. 2. To the Greeks I add the Hebrews, among whose most learned men this opinion has long prevailed, that קפוד is the hedgehog. R. Nathan explains it with the Spanish word ריצ"ו rizo, or erizo; Poniarius with the Italian ריצ"יו riccio; Rabbi Selomo with the French הריצ"ון herisson; Elias with the German איג"יל Igel. And in the Talmud קפוד kippod, or קופד kuphad, which is the same in the Chaldee inflection, is often placed among land quadrupeds. Thus in Berachoth, chapter 9, folio 57b: כל מיני חיות יפות לחלום חוץ מן הפיל והקוף והקפוד, All species of wild beasts are good for a dream (that is, of good omen when seen in sleep), except the elephant, the ape and the kippod, that is, the hedgehog. For R. Selomo talks nonsense when he explains it as the long-tailed monkey. And in the tractate Kelaim, ch. 8, folio 32a: והקופד וחולדת הסניים, And the kuphad (hedgehog) and the bramble weasel. And in Bava Kama, chapter 7: אין מגדלין חתולים וקופדים, They do not raise cats and kuphadim (hedgehogs). And in Sabbath, chapter 5, folio 57b: ואין העגל יוצא בגימון ולא פרא בעור הקופד, A calf may not go out (on the Sabbath) with a gemon, nor a cow with the skin of a kuphad. I think the Hebrew גימון gemon is κημὸν [kēmon], a muzzle, and that the word is derived from it; although by this term they do not mean any muzzle whatever, but the one by which a calf is prevented from sucking. The Aruch defines it: לוח בפיו שלא יוכל לשתות החלב, A board that is put in its mouth so that it cannot suck the milk. In Greek you would call it πύσσαχον [pyssachon]. Hesychius: Πύσσαχος· ξύλον καμπύλον τοῖς μόσχοις περὶ τοὺς μυκτῆρας τιθέμενον, ὃ κωλύει θηλάζειν· [Pyssachos; xylon kampylon tois moschois peri tous myktēras tithemenon, ho kōlyei thēlazein] A curved piece of wood placed around the nostrils of calves, by which they are prevented from sucking. And the skin of a kuphad (that is, of a hedgehog) was tied to the cow's udder for the same purpose, that is, so that neither the calf nor any other animal might suck it. Rabbi Selomo on this passage: קופד שרץ הוא שנימיו חדים כמחט וקורין לו הריצון וקושרין עורו בדדי הפרה שלא יניקוה שרצים, Kuphad is a creeping thing (so the Hebrews call the smallest quadrupeds) whose hairs are sharp like [col. 1037] needles; it is commonly called herisson. Its skin is tied to the cow's udder so that creeping things may not suck it. For the milk had to be guarded not from the calf alone, but also from serpents, among which boas are fed at first on the juice of cow's milk, whence they took their name. So Pliny, book 8, chapter 14. And Solinus, who follows him: It (the boa) lies in wait for herds of cattle, and fastens itself to the udder of whichever cow is most abundant in milk, and fattened by continual sucking, etc. 4. Finally, in Arabic قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud, plural قنافذ [qanāfidh] kanaphido, is the hedgehog. Barbarous translators write caused, ceufud, ceufund, etc. The matter is too well known to need proof. I will only advise the reader that the name قنفذ [qunfudh] kunphud includes, besides the hedgehog, also the porcupine. This is clear from Avicenna, who says that among the species of kunphud one is the mountain kind, having spines that can be shot, whose proper name is دلدل [duldul] duldul, that is, the porcupine. Hence in Damir the female hedgehog is called أم دلدل [umm duldul] mother τοῦ [tou] duldul, that is, of the porcupine. And duldul, or porcupine, is defined in the same place [II, 456] as عظيم القنافد [ʿaẓīm al-qanāfid], the larger hedgehog. And according to Algiahid: الفرق بين الدلدل والقنافد كالفرق بين البقر والجوامس والبخاتي من الابل العراب [al-farq bayna al-duldul wa-al-qanāfid ka-al-farq bayna al-baqar wa-al-jawāmis wa-al-bakhātī min al-ibil al-ʿirāb] Duldul and kanaphido (that is, the porcupine and hedgehogs properly so called) differ no otherwise than oxen from buffaloes, and Bactrian camels from Arabian ones. Finally Elmacinus, in the Saracen History, book 1, chapter 5, seems to have meant by القنفد [al-qunfud] alkunphud the porcupine rather than the hedgehog, when he writes of Aisha's camel: صار كالقنفد من السهام [ṣāra ka-al-qunfud min al-sihām] It became like an alkunphud from the darts, that is, from the multitude of darts with which it was pierced. But in this the Arabs had Pliny and Oppian to follow: the former, in book 8, chapter 35, expressly places porcupines in the hedgehog kind; the latter, in book 2 of the Cynegetica, line 603, making two kinds of land hedgehogs, some small and unwarlike, others μεγέθει πολὺ μείζονας [megethei poly meizonas], far larger, and bristling all round — ἀρειοτέρῃσιν ἀκωκαῖς [areioterēsin akōkais], with stronger points, seems to understand porcupines by those larger hedgehogs. And for Suidas too ἡ ὕστριξ [hē hystrix], the porcupine, is ὁ ἀκανθόχοιρος, ὁ χερσαῖος ἐχῖνος [ho akanthochoiros, ho chersaios echinos], the spiny pig, the land hedgehog.
